body_markdown:
Engines are dumb simple. Let me explain.


Back in the day, we needed something to replace the horse. Animals are pretty good for farm and transport work, but they are a bit hungry and leaky, and they sometimes die (they *do* have the ability to replicate themselves, however, which is a very redeeming trait). In 1908, the year Henry Ford introduced the[Model T](https://www.hagerty.com/media/market-trends/hagerty-insider/ever-popular-the-model-t-keeps-chugging-along/) , there were about 120,000 horses in New York City alone. Those animals deposited 2.5 million pounds of manure onto the mostly unpaved streets of Manhattan *per day* . The automobile was introduced as a pollution-reduction device, a novel concept for the climate activists of today.


Charles Phelps Cushing/Getty Images


So, how to make a portable fuel-burning device (as in *auto-mobility* ) that produced a little more power than a horse for doing useful things? Similar to how computers came about because of the critical mass of the transistor, pure-enough silicon, and photolithography, the internal combustion engine grew from cannons and steam engines in the late 1800s.


First, we needed something to blow up. Gunpowder was all over the place in the 1800s, but it was strictly a batch-burn, one-and-done process, even after someone put it inside a shell capped with a lead bullet. Liquids are much easier to move around and control, so many combustibles were considered. Viable candidates included kerosene (not so easy to vaporize) as well as gin and/or vodka (surprisingly good fuels and entertaining to quality-control), but we ended up with gasoline as the winner for a number of practical reasons. It is forgivably flammable and relatively easy to make, stores easily, and does not freeze (in the temperatures we experience on Earth, anyway)—those plus a hundred other reasons are why it emerged as the favorite.


Daily Herald Archive/Getty Images


Possibly gasoline’s most useful benefit is that you can have the air/fuel mixture off by 100% and it will still burn. One part of gasoline mixed with eight parts of air will ignite nicely, and so will about twice that amount of air. Gasoline is highly forgiving for how well (or poorly) it can mix with oxygen molecules; I have run cars down the road by spraying gasoline randomly from a Windex bottle into the intake manifold.


Norman H. Garrett


Early carburetors simply passed the intake air over an open bath of gasoline, which dutifully evaporated into the moving airstream to create a combustible mixture. Later we learned how to blend gasoline with specific evaporation characteristics that matched the depression (aka vacuum) that an engine makes on the intake stroke. We made a carburetor that used an internal low-pressure zone in a venturi to “boil off” the gasoline into a useful vaporous mixture. This robust process is still used today in many engines. The significant advancement of[fuel injection](https://www.hagerty.com/media/automotive-history/the-long-winding-road-to-efi/) , meanwhile, is analogous to an electronically controlled Windex bottle putting fuel where it needs to go—into the combustion space during the intake stroke (whether shot into the intake port or the cylinder itself, in the case of GDI).


Now that we had a powerful and usable fuel that didn’t freeze at 0°F and could still be useful on a hot summer day, we just needed a device to capture its chemical energy.


Lighting gasoline on fire makes heat energy, but we must be clever in how it is captured. We could simply burn the gasoline in an open pot, but the energy returned is pretty weak, really not much better than that of coal or wood. If we compress the air and fuel together, though, we get an exponential increase in power, so that became one of the foundations of the internal-combustion engine: Compress the mixture before blowing it up (this also works with gunpowder, which likes to be packed tightly, as any kid who has disassembled a firecracker and lit it off knows…).


Norman H. Garrett


A piston and a cylinder are an ideal pairing to compress the mixture, and we borrowed these from the aforementioned cannons and steam engines. Cannons taught us how to make smooth bores that hold great pressures (around 10,000 psi circa the War of 1812). *External* -combustion[steam engines](https://www.hagerty.com/media/people/the-work-and-life-of-the-man-who-invented-horsepower/) taught us how to do sequential processing of pressure cycles with pistons and cylinders, along with the all-important crankshaft and control valves. The crank and valves gave us a discrete way to separate the *internal* -combustion engine-to-be’s functions of the working chamber into A) intake; B) compression; C) explosion; and D) exhaust. This was familiar to cannoneers of the 1800s, who carried out the same four processes slowly and clumsily in a large weapon, albeit with gunpowder and a cannonball, which is analogous to our piston.


USPTO


With our piston in its bore, we can move it downward to suck air into the cylinder, creating one discrete process. The carburetor will automatically mix the gasoline into the air as it moves into the chamber. We can then close off the piston/cylinder cavity and change the cylinder’s function to compress the air/fuel mixture to any value we like (4-to-1 for the Model T; now up to 16-to-1 for race engines). This means we take, for example, 500 cc of air and gasoline vapor and squish it down to 50 cc (a 10:1 compression ratio) so that the fuel molecules are tightly packed against each other, all prepped for a chain reaction.


Henry Ford’s 1932 patent for an overhead-cam engine.


USPTO


Now that we have our compressed mixture all ready for explosion, we just need some energy to tip it over its critical point. A spark is wonderfully controllable, so that is our default ignition trigger. With a spark, we convert the working cylinder to yet another function: capturing the explosive force. It’s worth noting that fuel “ignition” can also come from over-compressing the air/fuel mixture so much that it reaches a critical temperature and explodes all on its own. This was Rudolph Diesel’s modus operandi, especially given that sparks were actually pretty hard to create reliably from batteries in 1897.


USPTO


USPTO


Spark away, as we are wont to do, and an explosion predictably occurs and forces the piston back down its cylinder bore. Luckily, that piston is not just a projectile, as a bullet or cannonball would be, but rather has its motion captured by the crankshaft, which collects the substantial energy in the motion driven by the pressure atop the piston’s head. The linear motion of the piston is literally “turned” into rotational motion, which conveniently matches the motion of the wheel we eventually want to activate.


When the explosion in the cylinder is over and the gasoline is all spent, we must do something with the ashes, so to speak. The crank is back at the ready, converting the piston from a projectile into a plunger, which, like a doctor’s syringe, pushes out the spent combustion byproducts. This is accomplished with a valve change (opening the exhaust port), which converts the cylinder bore to yet a fourth mode by exhausting all the spent gases and making the chamber ready for another go at it.


Norman H. Garrett


When the piston reaches the top of the exhaust stroke, the chamber is clear, and alternating valves once again change the function of the cylinder chamber back to being a suction device for the next intake stroke. Just like a cannoneer, we start another round. Since it takes one rotation for the ingestion and compression process, and it takes a second rotation to complete the explosion and exhaust process, we call it a four-stroke engine. Four strokes of the piston, but two rotations of the crank.


As I drive my old[MG TD](https://www.hagerty.com/media/driving/i-helped-make-the-first-miata-and-now-i-love-its-ancestor/) down the highway, the engine is running at a whopping 5500 revolutions per minute. That’s about 92 rotations per second, during which 46 combustion cycles happen across my four pistons and their cylinders—every second that passes. If you take the piston stroke into consideration, each piston travels about 37 miles up and down in one hour at that rpm. By contrast, my modern Audi A7 Quattro lopes along at 1800 rpm at 75 mph, thanks to its eight-speed transmission and goals of low engine friction via low cruising rpm (chasing the highest CAFE value possible). Each piston in my Audi has a similar-length stroke as my MG (about 3.5 inches) but only travels about 12 miles in that same hour, thanks to the lower engine speed. This is one of the many reasons modern engines’ rotating assemblies last to 200K miles and not 70K miles as we experienced in the ’60s.


Porsche


Modern engines are cloaked in all sorts of high technology, but at their core there is still just a simple piston and cylinder doing four cycles (with deference to Mazda’s rotary engines as the outstanding outlier). Just as the *Marvel* character Iron Man is just a guy covered in lots of gizmos, a modern engine is still a “Regular Joe” under all that tech. We have sensors and controllers and special systems and intelligent mechanisms ad nauseam that all but hide the modern engine from view, but underneath it is common to its roots: a crank, a piston, a cylinder, and some valves.


Even superchargers and turbos are akin to CPAP machines for our asthmatic Regular Joe, helping him breathe just a bit better for improved performance. Complexity moved our engines from the 60-horsepower-per-liter output of the 1950s to double that today. The shape of our engines has evolved over time, too, with inline, flat, opposed, V, and W configurations all finding a place underhood. But there have been no philosophical changes in the crank-rod-piston-cylinder head foundational idea dating back to 1908 (see graph below of power densities by decade, and once again shed a silent tear for the ’80s). Despite lots of NASA-level control systems and high-tech doodah, the humble rotating group of modern internal-combustion engines remains true to its 150-year-old roots.


Norman H. Garrett


That’s all there is to it. I tell my students that engines are simply dumb air pumps, and I make them repeat this in unison about once per lecture. How well we ingest the air is the major driver of how big an explosion can be made. Getting fuel into the cylinder is pretty easy, and the spark event is trivial to deliver. The magnitude of the explosion is tied, at its core, to the amount of air we got into the chamber on the intake stroke (technically, the moles of oxygen that we capture).


Race teams spend the lion’s share of their budgets on cylinder-head optimization; you must get the air in to get anything going. The subsequent explosion and the pressure on the piston determine how much torque we can create, which acts against the car’s inertia to get it moving. How fast we can repeat the process drives how much work we can do over a given amount of time against a load (e.g., finishing the work of accelerating in a short amount of time or pushing against our self-inflicted wind for a top speed run, as aerodynamic horsepower matches our engine’s output and a power balance is created).


[Brandan Gillogly](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/brandan-gillogly/)


It is all very simple. A piston in a cylinder typically can make *some* compression, the fuel ingested can be off by as much as 100% (air-fuel ratio of 8:1 to 16:1), and the spark can be 10 degrees too early or too late, and you’ll still probably get an engine to fire off. This latitude in engine operation gave the early inventors a lot of leeway in getting things started, literally.


Many, many advancements have happened since, and we are making three times the power we did a century ago, with negligible emissions, but the “first principles” are the same.


Next time you switch off your traction control and leave some “Elevens” in the parking lot, remember all that power under the hood is less mysterious than it seems, and give a nod to the lowly cannoneer and locomotive engineer who paved the way centuries ago.


***


*Norman Garrett was the concept engineer for the original Miata back in his days at Mazda’s Southern California Design Studio. When he’s not curating his small collection of dysfunctional automobiles and motorcycles, he teaches automotive engineering classes at UNC Charlotte’s Motorsports Engineering Department in North Carolina.*
